Equal Areas In Equilateral Triangle

GeometryTrianglesArea
Game: Move the point M inside the triangle and watch the six coloured pieces change.
How to play: Drag M, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Tick "names" or "hint" to see more, and press Reset to put M back.
Look for the math

Move M anywhere you like: the six pieces change shape, yet three of them always have exactly as much area as the other three. The two little bars under the picture show the two totals.

Six pieces, two groups

Let A′, B′ and C′ be the feet of the perpendiculars from M to BC, CA and AB. The six segments from M cut the equilateral triangle into six pieces. The green ones are AMB′, BMC′ and CMA′; the purple ones are A′MB, B′MC and C′MA. The claim on the cut-the-knot page is

Area(AMB′) + Area(BMC′) + Area(CMA′) = Area(A′MB) + Area(B′MC) + Area(C′MA).

The original applet coloured the six pieces red, grey, yellow, magenta, blue and dark orange. Here the same alternating pieces share two colours so the two groups are easy to follow.

Each piece is base times height

Every small triangle stands on part of a side of ABC, and its height is the distance from M to that side. Twice its area is just base × height. If the distances from M to BC, CA and AB are dA, dB, dC, then each distance times the whole side equals the same number: twice the area of ABC. This is Viviani's theorem: dA + dB + dC is always the altitude of ABC.

Write the position of M with three numbers a + b + c = 1, one for each vertex. Then dA = a × h, dB = b × h, dC = c × h, where h is the altitude. A perpendicular foot splits its side in a predictable way: on AB, for instance, the piece next to A has length (b + c/2) × side.

Why the totals are equal

Multiply those distances and pieces out. Adding the three green products gives

whole × (ab + bc + ca + (a² + b² + c²)/2),

where whole is twice the area of ABC. The purple products add up to exactly the same expression, because (a + b + c)² = 1. So each group is half of whole, which is the area of ABC. The logic test checks this at every point of a fine grid and at hundreds of random positions, and also compares every computed value with a second transcription of the applet's own bytecode.

Where the picture came from

The live cut-the-knot page now shows a still photograph in place of the Java applet; archived captures from 2010–2014 still embed EqualAreasInEquilateralTriangle. Its rules and its two checkboxes, "names" and "hint", are reproduced here. The hint draws the three parallels and their six right angles, as the page's proof suggests. One deliberate change: the Java applet stopped drawing when M was dragged outside, while here M simply stops at the edge; the claim is unchanged. Bogomolny thanks Manuel Silva of Portugal for bringing the problem to his attention.

Try moving M very close to a corner, then to the middle of a side. Watch the two bars: each keeps filling exactly half the width.
